newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Verbund HI net rise masks lower operating result.
newsitem.headline: Verbund HI net rise masks lower operating result.

text.p: Austrian national utility Verbund on Wednesday reported a 42 percent rise in first half group net profit, thanks to higher sales and a lower financial loss, but the figure masked a 20 percent drop in operating earnings.

Finance director Michael Pistauer said the company was aiming for a flat full-year result and was pinning its hopes for the second half on increased hydro electricity generation and stability in foreign currency markets.
"We expect water levels to improve in the second half and, provided there is no serious deterioration in foreign exchange rates, we should manage to match last year's excellent result," he said.
In 1995 Oesterreichische Elektrizitaetswirtschafts AG (Verbund), which supplies almost two-thirds of Austria's power needs, posted a group net profit of 1.38 billion schillings ($132.6 million).
This year, first half group net profit jumped 42 percent to 765.6 million schillings while pre-tax climbed 35 percent to 864 million.

Verbund traced the improvement to success in halving its financial loss to 716.8 million schillings. The firm said it had benefited from a depreciation of the Swiss franc which allowed it to draw on provisions of 350 million schillings.
Last year Verbund made provisions of 570 million schillings for foreign currency liabilities. About a fifth of Verbund bonds are denominated in Swiss francs.
Sales revenue rose 9.2 percent to 10.4 billion schillings, boosted by Austria's long cold winter and June 1995 price increases.
But operating profit slumped to 1.58 billion schillings from 1.98 billion as river levels fell and Verbund turned from cheap hydro electricity to thermal power.
An unfavourable electricity import deal with Hungary also took effect at the start of the year.
"Significantly increased fuel expenses and an increase in electricity purchase costs...were only partly offset by lower personnel expenses," Verbund said.

The company is taking legal action to try and annul the so-called Nagymaros agreement, which obliges Verbund to take 1.2 GigaWatt hours of Hungarian electricity annually for the next 20 years, although it does not need the power and the price makes resale difficult.
Investors were unimpressed by the results and Verbund shares closed 5.8 schillings down at 758.7 in a flat market.
"The net and pre-tax profit figures look good but there are still a couple of risk factors," said a Vienna trader, referring to the company's Swiss franc debt position.
Analysts said the decline in Verbund's operating profit was foreseeable. "It should not come as a surprise given the cold winter and low water levels," said Gerhard Auer from ICE Securities in London
He rated Verbund shares, which touched a life-high of 833 earlier this year, a "hold".
